svg.title: Three criteria for drawing domain boundaries, and why more domains stop paying for themselves
svg.desc: Domains are drawn on three criteria: the trust level of the assets, whether the compliance rules change across the boundary, and how far a compromise or failure would spread. The right-hand chart shows the isolation gained by adding one more domain falling while the cost of maintaining its policies stays roughly constant, so the two cross and every additional domain beyond that point buys almost nothing for the same maintenance burden.
svg.text: How many domains? Three criteria, then one economic question
Draw boundaries where the rules change, then check that each extra boundary still earns its maintenance
trust level — if this is compromised, what can the attacker do?
user endpoints (low) · servers (high value) · management (highest)
the domain is a statement about consequence, not about floor plan
compliance boundary — do the rules differ on either side?
cardholder data environment · domestic and foreign · production and test
this is the boundary that shrinks an audit, and it must be visible in the design
blast radius — how far does one failure or one compromise spread?
factory OT apart from office · production apart from test · supplier apart from staff
if the answer is "all the way", the two sides are already one domain
The question that decides the number
Every added domain buys isolation once, and then charges rent forever: one more policy set, one more failure point,
one more path to debug at three in the morning. So the useful question is not "how fine can we cut this" but
"does the next cut still pay for itself" — and that has an economic answer, drawn on the right.
GAIN AND COST OF ONE MORE DOMAIN
5–12 typical

The chart is illustrative, the shape is not: gain decays, cost does not. Enterprises land between five and twelve domains because that is where the two lines still separate.
